nodes.label: HamburgerMenu component
nodes.description: Collapsible nav menu for small viewports.

nodes.label: Instrument LSP round-trips
nodes.description: Wrap the WebSocket transport so every request is timed by method, with response size, and slow ones (over 50ms, or over 64KB) are logged in dev. Gives a before/after number for every later step instead of guessing. Measured outside the app already: identifier completions in this repo are ~1,000 items / 74 KB / 14-68 ms and complete (cached by the editor), import-path completions 15 items / 3 ms — so payload size is not the bottleneck and is not a step.

nodes.label: Drop the duplicate hover source
nodes.description: Every LSP editor gets hoverTooltips() twice: once inside the client's languageServerExtensions() (LSPClient.plugin includes client extensions per editor) and again via lspHoverTooltips in CodeEditorView.ViewModel's lspExtension. Each hover sends two textDocument/hover requests and builds two tooltips. Keep the client's one, remove the extra.

nodes.label: Dedupe Ctrl-hover definition lookups
nodes.description: modHoverDefinitionLink sends sync() + textDocument/definition on every mousemove while Ctrl is held, even over the same word. Cache the last word range per view and only ask again when the word under the pointer changes; keep the existing token guard for out-of-order responses.

nodes.label: Trim per-keystroke editor work
nodes.description: The editor's updateListener runs diagnosticCount() and a setProblemCount on every update, including cursor moves and focus changes. Recount only when the doc changed or a diagnostics transaction landed, so typing and arrowing don't touch React state they don't change.

nodes.label: Route tsserver responses per connection
nodes.description: The proxy binds every WebSocket connection's reader to the same tsserver stdout, so each connection receives every message: two windows' request ids collide, responses land in the wrong window, and the external server is killed when any one of its windows closes. Extract a router that rewrites request ids to be unique per server and maps responses back to their connection, broadcasts notifications, and ref-counts the external server. Also replace the per-chunk Buffer.concat deframer with a chunk list (minor at measured sizes, but quadratic on large messages).

nodes.label: Verify typing latency before/after
nodes.description: With the lspMetrics logging from step 1 on, type an import and an identifier in a Workspace TSX file and hover/Ctrl-hover a few symbols, before and after the steps above: compare hover requests per hover, definition requests per Ctrl-hover, and slow-request counts. Open two windows on the same project and confirm each only receives its own responses, and closing one keeps the other's code intelligence alive.

nodes.label: Rotate on the board

nodes.label: Rotation in the inspector and every emitter

nodes.label: Emit patterns compactly

nodes.label: Optimize along-path layout for big patterns

nodes.label: Path-flow editing on the board

nodes.label: Rotation geometry core

Promotes style.rotate (added for along-path) to a general, documented field for every layer kind.

nodes.label: Graph metrics core
nodes.description: One dependency-free module (node builtins only) that turns {files, import edges} into the numbers everything else uses: fan-in and fan-out per file, instability (fan-out / (fan-in + fan-out)), cycles via strongly connected components, dead files (no importers, not an entry point), hubs, clusters (label propagation) and reverse reachability for blast radius. Lives beside the other vendored CLIs so the app, the in-app agent and terminal agents all compute identical results — the AI never estimates a number.

nodes.label: Metrics on the Planning graph
nodes.description: Feed the edges Sleipnir already detects (importAdapters/detectEdges) through the metrics core, memoized per graph so a re-scan only recomputes what changed. Adds fan-in/fan-out, cycle membership and dead-file flags to graph nodes without changing the layout data. Zero tokens: purely local.

nodes.label: Health lens on the graph
nodes.description: An optional 'Health' view toggle beside ARCHITECTURE / PLAN ONLY, so the default all-white graph is untouched. With it on: node size grows with fan-in, counts (imports and imported-by) on hover or selection, cycles drawn red, wrong-direction imports amber, dead files faded. Visual rules live in a pure module so they are testable and theme tokens carry the colors in light and dark.

nodes.label: Readable large graphs
nodes.description: Big projects overlap today. Hide labels below a zoom level except for important nodes (high fan-in, selected, neighbours), collapse folders into single nodes with an aggregate count and expand on click, and keep the force layout stable when collapsing. Makes the health view legible at repo scale.

nodes.label: Health panel and blast radius
nodes.description: A panel next to the graph listing hubs, cycles, wrong-direction imports, dead files and (later) hotspots, each clickable to focus the graph. Selecting a file in the Health view lights up everything that depends on it, directly or not — its blast radius, for safer changes and faster debugging.

nodes.label: analyze_architecture agent tool
nodes.description: An in-app agent tool that runs the metrics core on the open project and returns a compact, capped report (top 20 hubs, every cycle up to a limit, violations, hotspots, per-file counts on request) — a few thousand tokens instead of source code. The agent then reads only the files it decides to change. Scoping by folder and a goal keep it smaller still.

nodes.label: Flow beyond imports
nodes.description: Map logic flow that imports don't show: Electron IPC channels (ipcMain.handle with invoke), HTTP routes (frontend fetch of /api/x with the backend route, across languages), and event emit/on pairs. New edge kinds drawn with their own line styles (dashed IPC, dotted events), included in the metrics and the optimize report, so async and cross-language systems are analyzed as one graph.

nodes.label: Feature finder
nodes.description: Turn '/optimize my right click menu' into the feature's own sub-graph: seed files from a name and behaviour search (component names, handlers like onContextMenu, strings, routes), then grow along imports (what it uses) and importers (where it is mounted), ranked by graph distance and fan-in, capped to ~15 files. Narrows what the agent reads (fewer tokens, better focus) and is drawn on the graph as the scope of the run.

nodes.label: Measurement harness
nodes.description: Measure before changing anything, the same way every time: interaction timing in the running app or a preview over the DevTools Protocol (time from input to paint, long tasks, React re-render counts) and per-language micro-benchmarks (Vitest bench, Rust criterion, Go testing.B, pytest-benchmark). Several runs, median and spread reported, so noise is never mistaken for a win. A measurement can be saved as a performance test with a budget that the Validation view enforces.

nodes.label: Optimization loop
nodes.description: '/optimize <feature> and try it': baseline, then rounds of one hypothesis, one small change, tests as the correctness gate, re-measure, keep only if it beats the baseline by more than the noise, otherwise undo. Each kept change is a reviewable change set. Capped rounds and token budget, stops early when nothing helps, never pushes. Hypotheses come from a pattern catalog (state lifted too high causing re-renders, sync work in handlers, missing memoization, heavy imports on the hot path, N+1 calls) plus the graph signals.

nodes.label: Optimize results card
nodes.description: A report in the chat and on the plan: baseline and final numbers (menu open 180ms to 45ms, re-renders 40 to 3), every attempt with its measurement and whether it was kept or undone, the files touched highlighted on the graph, and the saved performance budget. Makes the agent's work inspectable and repeatable.

nodes.label: Test and pipeline failures on the graph
nodes.description: Map failing tests and CI runs (Vitest results, GitHub Actions job logs) onto the graph: a failure lights its test file and import path, and suspects are ranked by blast radius, recent churn, co-change history (files that change together without importing each other) and what changed since the last green run. Also predictive test selection: run only the tests whose import closure touches the change, for faster loops in /optimize and everyday work.

nodes.label: One language registry
nodes.description: A language is defined in eight places today (architectures.ts LANGUAGES, planDoc EXT_LANGUAGE, the importAdapters and codeEditorLanguages ext maps, analyze.mjs SOURCE_EXT, runTargets, lsp-proxy, templates), so adding C means touching all of them and they drift. One pure-data registry with no imports (like graphCore.mjs), usable by the renderer, Electron and the vendored CLIs. Per language: id, label, extensions, comment syntax (line, block, hash, html), header/source split (C, C++), the manifests that detect it, file-naming convention (camel, snake, Pascal), editor grammar, language server (command, args, install hint), build/run/test commands, .gitignore entries, and the UI frameworks a canvas component can target in it. Seeds: TypeScript, React, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go, C, C++, Java, Kotlin, Swift, C#, HTML, CSS; frameworks React, Vue, Svelte, HTML, Leptos, Dioxus, templ, LVGL, SwiftUI. Consumers wired in this step: architectures.ts derives LANGUAGES from it; syncPlanDoc inlines it into the vendored plan.mjs (which stays import-free); analyze.mjs reads its extensions; the scaffolder vendors it as .sleipnir/languages.mjs. Test: every consumer agrees with the registry.

nodes.label: Detect C, C++, Java, Swift and C# projects
nodes.description: detect-project reads manifests from the registry instead of its own list: CMakeLists.txt, Makefile or meson.build become c or cpp (by the sources present) and are supported rather than reported as unsupported; pom.xml and build.gradle(.kts) become java or kotlin; Package.swift becomes swift; .csproj/.sln become csharp. conventions reports each language source and include folders (src + include for C, src/main/java for Java), so agents running /plan put files where the project expects them. Mixed repos (a Rust core with a React UI) keep a language per folder. AGENTS.md lists every language extension for planned files.

nodes.label: Scaffold any language in Planning
nodes.description: Role templates for C, C++, Java, Kotlin, Swift and C# beside the existing TypeScript, Python, Rust and Go ones, chosen from the registry. C and C++ split by role: the Interface role is the header (.h/.hpp) and every other role is a source file that includes its own header, so a C view includes view_model.h the way a TSX view imports its ViewModel. File names follow each language convention (cart_view.c, CartView.java, cart_view.rs). The Add Node language picker lists every registered language; non-architectural ones (CSS) still scaffold single files. Test: every language x role renders with balanced braces and include guards, and siblings link.

nodes.label: Imports and Health for C, C++, Java, Kotlin, Swift, C#
nodes.description: Real import resolution so the architecture graph and the Health view work for these languages instead of the basename-guessing fallback. C/C++: #include "x.h" relative to the file, then include dirs from compile_commands.json or CMake include_directories, with header and source paired as one unit. Java/Kotlin: package + import to a path under src/main/java or kotlin. Swift and C#: module and namespace, same-module types by folder. analyze.mjs gets the same parsers (vendored, pure), and graphCore roles learn them: headers are the interface layer, main.c, Main.java and Program.cs are entries, *_test.c and *Test.java are tests. Lab: add a CMake fixture with an include cycle and a Gradle fixture with a misplaced class to tools/optimizeLab.

nodes.label: Workspace: highlighting for every language
nodes.description: codeEditorLanguages reads the registry. Adds @codemirror/lang-cpp (C, C++), @codemirror/lang-java, and @codemirror/legacy-modes StreamLanguage modes for Swift, Kotlin, C#, TOML, YAML, shell and CMake. Grammars load on demand with a dynamic import so none of them reaches the first load. The duplicate extension maps in codeEditorLanguages and importAdapters collapse into the registry. Unknown extensions still open as plain editable text.

nodes.label: Workspace: a language server per language
nodes.description: lsp-proxy only spawns typescript-language-server. Generalize it to the registry server per language: clangd (C, C++), rust-analyzer, gopls, pyright-langserver or pylsp, jdtls, kotlin-language-server, sourcekit-lsp, csharp-ls. Each is found on PATH (or a configured path), started lazily the first time a file of that language opens, one per project root and language, and stopped when the project closes. The editor client connects per language. A missing server is a quiet status line with the install command from the registry, never an error dialog. The self-host tsserver special case stays.

nodes.label: Workspace: build, run and test any project
nodes.description: Play finds CMake (configure, build, run the target), Make, Meson, Gradle/Maven, SwiftPM and dotnet projects next to npm, cargo, go and python. Validation, Vitest-only today, runs each language test runner from the registry (cargo test, go test -json, pytest with junit output, ctest, gradle test, swift test, dotnet test) and parses all of them into one result shape: suite, test, status, duration, failure message with file:line. The Validation view, and later the Health view failure overlay, then read any language the same way.

nodes.label: Git: language-aware diffs and ignores
nodes.description: Diffs are plain text today. Highlight hunks with the file grammar from the registry (static Lezer highlighting, no editor instance per hunk). Lockfiles and generated output (Cargo.lock, go.sum, package-lock.json, build folders) collapse by default. initRepo writes a .gitignore built from the detected languages (target/, build/, __pycache__/, .venv/, *.o, out/, bin/ and obj/), and Source Control offers to add a missing ignore when build output shows up as untracked. Note: src/06_source_control is being edited in parallel; start from that work.

nodes.label: Canvas: pick the language on the element
nodes.description: LANGUAGES.md stages 1 and 2. A component TARGET is dead data today: everything emits React. Stage 1: region sentinels take a closed comment-style id (line-slash, block-slash, html, plus hash for Python and TOML shaped targets), defaulting to today // so every file on disk keeps working; region.test.ts must pass unmodified. Stage 2: a CanvasEmitter interface (extension, comment style, indent, fileName, symbol, emitRegionBody, collectImports, emitComponentFile, and the property support table used next), an emitter registry with no fallback (React into a file meant to be HTML is worse than nothing), targets derived from the emitter registry crossed with the language registry, and the inspector TARGET dropdown wired on the element itself, locked once the component has a file. React moves behind the interface with byte-identical output.

nodes.label: The Frame spec: canvas properties as the cross-language contract
nodes.description: Decision: the base Frame is a spec, not a runtime. CanvasStyle already is the one box model (layout, sizing, paint, effects, rotation, along-path). frameSpec lists every property once with its meaning, units and default, and each emitter declares per property: exact, approximate (with the reason) or unsupported. The inspector reads it for the selected element target, so an unsupported property is greyed with its reason (per-corner radius: approximate in SwiftUI) and the design never promises what the code cannot do. Every lowering stays a pure function of the same IR, so adding a language never touches the others. Record the decisions (spec over runtime, the CSS policy, the motion and 3D direction) in LANGUAGES.md.

nodes.label: React Frame mode: canvas properties as code props (opt-in)
nodes.description: For code that reads like the inspector: emit <Frame flow="vertical" gap={8} fill={...}> instead of divs with style objects. The Frame is copied into the project (src/components/Frame/, owned by the user like shadcn components, no Sleipnir dependency) from UIKit Frame on first use and kept current by a version stamp. toFrameProps (CanvasStyle to FrameProps; removed as unused, restore from 9f835de^) is the mapping, and reading code back onto the canvas becomes reading props. Off by default: plain divs stay the zero-dependency default, and other languages always use static lowering, because the Frame runs toCss at runtime and porting that derivation into every language would recreate the drift the spec avoids.

nodes.label: Stylesheets: multi-file components and the CSS policy
nodes.description: Policy: inline until inline cannot. React keeps inline style objects (exact, one file) unless a component needs what inline cannot express (hover, press and focus states, breakpoints, keyframe animation); then it gets a co-located Card.module.css with one class per node. Markup-first targets (HTML, Vue, Svelte, templ, Leptos) always use a stylesheet. Theme tokens become CSS variables, so components follow the app theme. Needs LANGUAGES.md phase 2: CanvasComponent.outputs[] (target, files, sync, per-file hashes), schema v2 with an idempotent migration, and cssDeclarations() in toCss (kebab-case, px on unitless numbers except opacity, flex, fontWeight, lineHeight, zIndex). One derivation still feeds the board and the code.

nodes.label: Web targets: HTML, Vue, Svelte
nodes.description: LANGUAGES.md stages 3 and 4, plus Svelte. HTML: one document, region inside <body>, variants as hidden siblings, nested instances inlined with a cycle guard. Vue SFC: html-style sentinel inside <template> (never //), v-if variants, real component imports that keep their extension. Svelte: {#if} variants and a scoped <style>. All three use the step 12 stylesheet, so the board preview stays exact. Acceptance: one board with React, HTML and Vue components side by side, each pushed with its own sentinel style and tracked dirty independently.

nodes.label: Rust and Go components: Leptos and templ
nodes.description: Rust and Go reach the canvas through web UI frameworks that keep the CSS box model, so the preview stays exact. Rust: a Leptos component (a #[component] fn returning view! markup, classes from the component stylesheet, props as a struct), with Dioxus rsx! as a second Rust emitter on the same lowering. Go: a templ component with a props struct. Variants become a Rust enum with match and a Go switch. File naming and comment sentinels come from the registry (snake_case .rs, // regions); a Rust component lands in the crate components module and is registered in mod.rs.

nodes.label: Native targets: C (LVGL) and SwiftUI
nodes.description: Toolkits without CSS need a second lowering. toNative maps the IR to a layout tree (flex flow, gap, padding, alignment, fixed, hug and fill sizes, absolute children) and records every divergence. LVGL, the C UI toolkit with real flex layout for embedded and desktop, emits card.h (a props struct and a create function) and card.c (lv_obj calls, one lv_style_t per node, flex flow and align, radius, border, shadow). SwiftUI emits stacks and modifiers per LANGUAGES.md stage 5 (.offset, never .position). The board cannot render these natively, so a native-target component wears an approximate-preview badge and the inspector shows its frameSpec divergences. C without a UI toolkit still gets no frame, but can get its props struct.

nodes.label: AI commands in any language
nodes.description: For "/component a pricing card in Vue" or "/plan a sensor driver in C": canvas.mjs build and the canvas_build tool take a target, validated against the available emitters and answered with the unavailable reason instead of quietly falling back to React. The /plan and /optimize skills tell agents to read detect-project languages and plan each folder in its own language. The chat slash hints show the language argument.

nodes.label: Motion: states, transitions and keyframes
nodes.description: The IR gets a time axis. Interaction states (hover, press, focus) are style overrides like variants; transitions say how each property moves between them (duration, easing, delay); keyframe timelines animate opacity, rotate, position, scale and fills, plus motion along a path that reuses pathFlow. The board previews with the Web Animations API on the same toCss values, and a timeline panel scrubs and plays. Lowering: web targets get CSS transitions and @keyframes in the component stylesheet (why stylesheets come first), React Frame mode a motion prop, SwiftUI .animation and withAnimation, LVGL lv_anim_t; each declared in frameSpec, unsupported shown with its reason. Emitted CSS honors prefers-reduced-motion.

nodes.label: 3D: scene nodes
nodes.description: A new layer kind: a frame that holds a 3D scene with primitives (box, sphere, plane, torus), glTF models from .components/assets, a camera, lights, and materials taken from canvas fills. It is positioned and laid out like any frame, so a 3D hero sits inside a 2D page. The board renders it with three.js through @react-three/fiber, loaded on demand with a dynamic import so three.js never reaches the first load. Motion keyframes drive object transforms and the camera. Emit: React gets an R3F component, web markup targets a small vanilla three.js module, native targets unsupported with the reason (SceneKit or RealityKit later for Swift).

nodes.label: Geometry kernel: every layer is a shape
nodes.description: The bridge between 2D and 3D. Every layer already has an outline: a frame is a (per-corner) rounded rectangle, an ellipse is an ellipse, a polygon or star is a polygon, a vector is Bezier paths, an image is its box. One Shape type holds that outline as closed contours; flattening turns curves into polygons at a chosen tolerance, and triangulation (earcut, holes included) turns polygons into a flat mesh. Pure and tested, with no renderer: the 2D board can use it for exact hit-testing and boolean ops, and every 3D step builds on it. A 2D design is then literally a 3D scene seen from the front with every layer at depth 0.

nodes.label: Depth on every layer: extrude, revolve, sweep
nodes.description: Any frame or vector can leave the plane: a 3D transform (z, tilt on x and y, depth scale) and a shape modifier. Extrude gives a 2D outline thickness and bevels; revolve spins it around an axis into a lathe (vase, wheel, bottle); sweep runs it along a guide path, reusing pathGuide, into tubes and ribbons. A logo becomes a 3D object in two clicks and stays editable as 2D: the outline is still the source. The board gets a 2D/3D toggle: 2D is the orthographic front view of the same scene, 3D orbits it, so nothing is converted and nothing is lost going back.

nodes.label: Materials and shading
nodes.description: Physically based materials per layer that start from what the layer already has: a solid fill becomes base color, an image fill a texture map, a gradient a generated texture, opacity becomes transmission. Add metalness, roughness, emissive, clearcoat and normal maps, plus lights and an environment (HDRI) for the scene. Then a node-based shader editor drawn with the same graph engine as Planning: texture, math, noise and mix nodes compiled to three.js node materials (TSL, which targets both WebGL and WebGPU). Materials are assets in .components/, reusable across layers and boards.

nodes.label: Polygon modelling
nodes.description: An edit mode for meshes: select vertices, edges and faces; move, rotate and scale them; extrude and inset faces, bevel edges, loop cut, merge, mirror, and subdivision surfaces for smooth forms. Booleans (union, subtract, intersect) between any two solids with a CSG library (three-bvh-csg). A modelled mesh keeps its history as an ordered modifier stack on top of the 2D outline it came from, so an edit can be revisited, and it shares the canvas undo. Mesh data lives in the board document (positions, faces, UVs), saved compactly.

nodes.label: 3D export and code
nodes.description: Get models out: glTF/GLB (with materials), OBJ, and STL for 3D printing, from a layer, a selection or a scene; import glTF and OBJ back as editable meshes. Code: a React Three Fiber component per 3D component and a plain three.js module for web targets, through the same emitter registry as 2D. And the other direction: render a 3D view out as an SVG or PNG layer, so a modelled object can drop back into a flat design.

nodes.label: 3D scene model: placements, solids and storage
nodes.description: The data underneath everything else. Every layer can carry a 3D placement (position, rotation as a quaternion, scale), and a frame can be a sketch plane: XY (front), XZ (top), YZ (side), or any of those rotated about any axis, its 2D contents living on that plane. New layer kinds: a 3D component (a group of solids, lights and cameras placed in space, built on the board like any frame) and a solid (an outline plus its modifier stack, or an edited mesh). Units are meters with Y up, the glTF convention, so export needs no guessing. Heavy mesh data lives in binary assets (.components/assets/*.glb) referenced from the board, so board JSON stays small and diffable. Schema bump with an idempotent migration; undo covers every 3D edit.

nodes.label: The 3D viewport and the 2D/3D toggle
nodes.description: A three.js viewport on the board (React Three Fiber, already a dependency, loaded on demand so it never touches the first load), WebGPU where available and WebGL otherwise. One toggle swaps the board between 2D and 3D: 2D is the orthographic straight-on view of the plane being edited, 3D orbits the same scene, so nothing is converted going back and forth. Front, Top, Side and Perspective views, a grid and axis gizmo, move/rotate/scale handles, frame-selection shared with the layers panel, and every 2D layer drawn as a flat mesh through the geometry kernel (shape.ts, mesh.ts) so a flat design looks identical in both views.

nodes.label: Sketch planes: frames on XY, XZ, YZ or any angle
nodes.description: Put any frame on a plane from the inspector (Front, Top, Side, or a custom rotation and offset) and it stands in the 3D scene at that orientation. Editing a plane opens it straight-on in 2D, with the board tools unchanged: the SVG and frame tools become the sketch tools. Cross-plane guides make orthographic sketching work: points drawn on Front project as guide lines onto Top and Side (shared X, Y or Z), so the three views of one object line up like blueprint views. Reference images can be pinned to a plane at real size.

nodes.label: Solids from one sketch: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft
nodes.description: An outline on a plane becomes a solid through a modifier: extrude (depth, bevel size and segments, taper), revolve (axis, angle, steps: vases, wheels, bottles), sweep (along a guide path, reusing pathGuide: pipes, rails, ribbons) and loft (through two or more profiles on parallel planes: fuselages, bottles with varying section). How points map to polygons is explicit and shown: each sketch anchor is a vertex of the profile, curves are split at the flattening tolerance, and the polygon count is profile vertices x the segments the modifier adds (extrude depth segments, revolve steps, sweep samples). Loft needs matching point counts, so profiles are resampled to the same count with their anchors kept. A live polygon and triangle count sits in the inspector. The sketch stays the source: edit it and the solid rebuilds.

nodes.label: Solids from Top, Front and Side sketches, and booleans
nodes.description: Three orthographic silhouettes become one solid by carving: extrude the Front sketch through the depth, the Side across the width, the Top down the height, and intersect the three (the visual hull). Booleans (union, subtract, intersect) between any solids use three-bvh-csg. What views alone cannot tell is stated in the UI, not hidden: a hollow no silhouette shows (a bowl, a cup interior), and curvature between views (three circles carve a Steinmetz solid, not a sphere). The fixes are built in: add section sketches on more planes and loft through them, subtract a carved cavity, or refine in edit mode and sculpting.

nodes.label: Editable meshes
nodes.description: Apply a modifier stack to get a mesh you can edit by hand: a half-edge mesh with n-gon faces (quads stay quads, which subdivision and engines prefer), hard and smooth edges, vertex normals, UV layers and vertex colors. Kept in a .glb asset with its history recorded, so an applied solid can still be traced to the sketch it came from. Validation keeps meshes engine-ready: manifold checks, no degenerate faces, consistent winding.

nodes.label: Edit mode: vertices, edges, faces
nodes.description: Polygon modelling on the editable mesh: select vertices, edges or faces (click, box, loop and ring selection), move, rotate and scale them with the gizmo, extrude and inset faces, bevel edges and vertices, loop cut, knife, merge, bridge edge loops, fill holes, and mirror with symmetry across an axis. Every operation is one undo step through the canvas undo stack, and works in the orthographic views as well as perspective.

nodes.label: Subdivision, decimation and polygon budgets
nodes.description: Catmull-Clark subdivision as a modifier with per-edge crease weights, so a low-poly cage reads as a smooth form (the standard way to model cars, characters, product shots). Decimate and quad-remesh to bring a dense mesh to a game budget, with a budget readout per object and per scene (triangles, vertices, draw calls) against targets for web, mobile and desktop engines.

nodes.label: Sculpting
nodes.description: For organic detail sketches and polygon edits can not reach: brushes on a dense mesh (draw, clay, grab, smooth, inflate, crease, flatten, pinch), with radius, strength, falloff, pen pressure and mirror symmetry. Dense meshes come from a voxel remesh of any solid or from multiresolution subdivision, so a sculpt can start from a sketched base. Detail bakes down to a normal map on the low-poly mesh for engines. Brushes run on the GPU where available and a BVH keeps strokes interactive on hundreds of thousands of faces.

nodes.label: UVs and textures
nodes.description: Every solid gets usable UVs: a sketch-plane projection by default (the plane it was drawn on is the natural mapping, so an image fill lands where it showed in 2D), plus automatic unwrapping with seams (xatlas compiled to WebAssembly) and a UV editor drawn on the 2D board. Image fills become textures; normal, roughness, metalness and ambient-occlusion maps attach to material slots; baking lights and sculpt detail into textures follows.

nodes.label: Materials and node shading
nodes.description: Physically based materials that start from what a layer already has (solid fill to base color, image fill to texture, gradient to a generated texture, opacity to transmission) plus metalness, roughness, emissive, clearcoat, sheen and normal maps. A node shader editor drawn with the same graph engine as Planning: texture, noise, math, mix, fresnel and time nodes compiled to three.js node materials (TSL), which target WebGPU and WebGL from one graph. Materials are reusable assets in .components/materials and export as glTF materials (with the nodes baked where glTF has no equivalent).

nodes.label: Environments: lights, cameras, world
nodes.description: What turns objects into a place: point, spot, directional and area lights with soft shadows, an HDRI environment and sky, fog, a ground plane, and cameras with focal length and depth of field that can be looked through and animated. Scatter and instancing reuse the 2D pattern tools (pathPattern) in 3D: trees along a path, rocks across a surface, as GPU instances. Levels of detail per object keep large scenes fast.

nodes.label: Armatures and skinning
nodes.description: Bones for characters and mechanisms: an armature drawn bone by bone on sketch planes (so a side-view sketch can carry a spine and a front view the arms), with parenting, roll and constraints (IK chains, look-at, copy rotation). Skinning binds a mesh to bones with automatic weights from bone distance and heat diffusion, then a weight-paint brush refines them; pose mode tests deformation. Exports as glTF skins.

nodes.label: Animation
nodes.description: One timeline for 2D and 3D: keyframes on transforms, bone poses, material parameters, light and camera properties, and shape keys (morph targets) for facial and squash-and-stretch animation. Curve editor with easing and tangents, named clips (walk, idle, open-door) that play, loop and blend, and onion skinning in 2D views. Motion along a path reuses pathFlow. Clips export as glTF animations so engines play them by name.

nodes.label: Functional environments: physics and interaction
nodes.description: Scenes that can be played, not only looked at: rigid bodies and colliders (box, sphere, capsule, convex hull, mesh) with Rapier compiled to WebAssembly, triggers, joints, and a play mode in the viewport. Interaction states shared with 2D UI (hover, press, focus) drive 3D objects, so a door opens on click and a panel lights up on hover. 3D UI: any 2D frame can sit in the scene as a panel, HUD or screen that stays crisp (rendered from the same box model), for in-world interfaces.

nodes.label: Export and import: glTF, USD, OBJ, STL
nodes.description: Get work into every engine with standard files rather than generated engine code: glTF/GLB with meshes, PBR materials, skins, morph targets, animations, lights and cameras; USD/USDZ for Apple and film pipelines; OBJ and STL for printing. Export presets set the axis and unit conventions each engine wants (Unreal Z-up centimeters, Unity and Godot Y-up meters). Import glTF, OBJ and FBX back as editable meshes. Round-trip tests check that what leaves Sleipnir comes back the same.

nodes.label: 3D components as code
nodes.description: A 3D component becomes code like a 2D one does, through the emitter registry: a React Three Fiber component that loads its .glb and wires its interaction states and animation clips, or a plain three.js module for non-React web pages. 2D UI and 3D scenes mix in one component tree, so a product page with a live 3D model is one design.

nodes.label: AI can model too
nodes.description: Teach the /frame, /component and canvas_build tools 3D: a spec can place frames on planes, sketch profiles, apply extrude, revolve, loft and carve, assign materials, add lights, and build an armature. The agent can then rough out a blockout from a description ("a low-poly lighthouse on a rock"), and the result is ordinary editable sketches and modifiers, not a frozen mesh. A /model command routes to it.

nodes.label: Point selection: transform just the points you pick
nodes.description: Select only some points of any shape and move, rotate or scale them on their own, about a pivot you can place (their center by default, or any point, anchor or layer). Works on every vector, and on frames and components through their outline: a frame or component edited by points becomes a path that keeps its fills, strokes and children. Box, lasso, shift and loop selection of points; rotation and scale handles around the selection; numeric rotate in the inspector. For components, an instance can be rotated or have points moved as its own override, without touching the main component or its other instances. The same selection model (points, then edges and faces) carries straight into 3D edit mode and the sculpt brushes.

nodes.label: Quick sculpt brushes in the pen toolbox
nodes.description: A few simple brushes beside the pen tool in the bottom toolbox, for shaping without leaving the board: push, pull, smooth, inflate and pinch, with one radius and strength (pen pressure when there is one). On a 2D vector they move the points under the brush with a soft falloff, adding points where the curve needs them, so a hand-drawn shape can be nudged organically. On a 3D solid they are the light versions of the full sculpt brushes, working on the surface directly. Same selection model as point editing, so a brush can be limited to selected points.

nodes.label: The inspector in 3D: alignment, fill, stroke
nodes.description: The same inspector sections work on 3D objects, meaning the same thing in space. Alignment: align and distribute along X, Y or Z, to the selection, a parent component or the ground, and snap to faces, edges and other objects. Fill is the surface: the fill list becomes the material stack (a solid fill to base color, an image to a texture, opacity to transmission), shaded by the scene lights. Stroke is the outline: a stroke draws the object edges or silhouette in 3D with its color and weight in pixels or world units, for stylized, toon and technical-drawing looks, and inside/center/outside keeps its meaning against the silhouette. Effects map too: drop shadow to cast shadows, blur to depth of field. One inspector, so moving between 2D and 3D asks nothing new.

nodes.label: Studio: the Analytics slot becomes lighting, materials and animation
nodes.description: Long term: the hidden Analytics section (src/05_analytics) is replaced by Studio, a workspace for finishing a 3D scene rather than building it. A large viewport with lighting tools (key, fill and rim presets, HDRI picker, light linking, exposure and tone mapping), a material library and the node shader editor side by side, and the animation timeline with clips, curves and camera shots, plus a render panel for stills and turntable or shot videos. It works on the same boards and components as the Canvas, so a model goes from sketch to lit, animated shot without export.

nodes.label: One status, the agent’s: pending, in progress, completed
nodes.description: Planning carries two status systems today: a step’s approval (draft, approved, done) and a separate stage (proposed, in progress, in review, done), kept in step by useStatusReconciler. Replace both with the three states AI agents already track their own work in (Claude Code’s todo list, Codex and Gemini plans): pending, in progress, completed. Approval stays, but as an action (a human saying go, which marks the step in progress and lets Sleipnir write its planned files), not a fourth status. Glyphs: dashed ring, ring with a soft pulse, solid dot. Old boards migrate on read and idempotently: proposed and draft to pending, in progress, in review and approved to in progress, done to completed.

nodes.label: Agents report their progress on the plan
nodes.description: The plan reflects what the agent is actually doing, from the agent itself. The plan CLI gets set-status (a step id, pending, in progress or completed, and an optional one-line note of what it did), and the in-app agent an update_plan_step tool. The /plan and /optimize skills tell agents to keep the plan as their working todo list: one step in progress at a time, completed the moment it is done, with the note. The graph updates live through the planning watcher, so watching a plan is watching the agent work.

nodes.label: Every AI change, recorded against its step
nodes.description: A per-plan activity log in .planning/<plan>/activity.json: for each step, when it started and finished, which agent worked it, and every file it created, changed or deleted. The in-app agent writes its change sets there (changeSets.cjs already records them, with undo). For terminal agents Sleipnir attributes changes itself: a workspace snapshot when a step goes in progress, compared when it completes, so even an agent that never reports files is accounted for. A step’s card lists its changes with diffs, and the files light up on the architecture graph.

nodes.label: Live agent activity on the graph
nodes.description: Diagnostics in real time: while an agent works, its current step pulses, and the files it reads and writes flash on the architecture graph as it touches them, so you see where its attention is and whether it is wandering outside the plan. In-app agent tool calls (read_file, generate_code, run_command) stream as events; terminal agents are followed through file-system changes attributed to the step in progress. A slim strip under the graph names the agent, the step, the time on it, and the last few actions, with a link into the full log.

nodes.label: Skills: the skill tree
nodes.description: A SKILLS view in Planning, drawn with the same graph: every skill an agent in this project can run, built in (/plan, /optimize, /frame, /component) or the user’s own, found where each agent keeps them (Claude Code’s .claude/commands and .claude/skills, Codex’s .codex/prompts, Gemini’s .gemini/commands). Each skill links to the tools and CLIs it drives (plan.mjs, canvas.mjs, analyze.mjs) and to what it writes (.planning, boards, code), so you can see what a skill can touch before an agent runs it. Filter by agent to see what Claude, Codex or Gemini each have.

nodes.label: Edit and add skills, per agent
nodes.description: Open any skill’s file in the editor. New skill: a name, a description, the instructions, and which agents get it; Sleipnir writes each agent’s own format (Markdown with frontmatter for Claude and Codex, TOML for Gemini) through the same emitters that write the built-in ones. A built-in skill is changed through a project override in .sleipnir/skills/<id>.md that the scaffolder merges, so the change survives updates instead of being overwritten.

nodes.label: Planning organized around the agent
nodes.description: Planning becomes the place to watch and steer agents: PLANS (ongoing plans over the architecture, with live status and activity), SKILLS (the skill tree) and HEALTH (the architecture lens), one tab strip. The header shows any agent run in progress: which plan and step, how long, how many files touched. Manual node creation stays available but steps back: the human role here is reviewing, approving and redirecting, not filling in nodes by hand.

nodes.label: Tests clean up their step snapshots
nodes.description: Step snapshots live in the OS temp folder, and the planning tests leave theirs behind for every temp project they create. Remove each test project's snapshot folder when the test finishes.

nodes.label: list-steps shows what each finished step changed
nodes.description: list-steps prints, for a finished step, how many files it changed, so an agent picking up a plan sees what each step touched without opening the activity log.

nodes.label: Slim the always-loaded instructions
nodes.description: AGENTS.md costs about 3,100 tokens in every session. Keep only what every session needs there (the plan CLI's commands, reporting progress, where to read what people said) and move the rest where it loads only when used: planned-file rules into /plan, Canvas into /frame and /component, analyzer detail into /optimize, the rest into the CLI's --help. Target: about 500 tokens.

nodes.label: What people say on a node, agents read
nodes.description: A status set or a comment written on a step's card reaches the agent exactly as its own reports do: it's in the plan's activity log, in plan.md under the step, and in list-steps — which agents are told to read before they work a step. A comment box on the step card; a comment command in the CLI for agents to answer.

nodes.label: The agent trail: watch, not report
nodes.description: Record what agents do without spending their tokens: a silent Claude Code hook logs every tool call (reads, edits, commands) to .planning/trail.jsonl, the in-app agent logs its own tool calls there, and file-system watching covers any other agent's edits. Git-ignored, capped, per session.

nodes.label: The trail on the graph
nodes.description: The agent's path through the network, live: files it reads glow briefly, files it edits pulse blue, files its tests run flash orange, and a fading line follows the order it went — the visible shape of the agent's thinking.

nodes.label: Measure: tokens with and without watching
nodes.description: Re-run the same headless Claude Code task with the slim instructions and the trail hook on and off, at the same effort, and report what each costs — the target is no added tokens for watching.

nodes.label: A corner box where the agent is working
nodes.description: Replace the trail's glows and the orange testing tone with one mark: four corner brackets (⌜⌝⌞⌟) drawn as an SVG box around the node the agent is on, blinking while it's there — white while it reads, searches or thinks, blue while it edits or runs tests (a quicker blink for tests) — fading over a few seconds once it moves on. A step being tested keeps its blue ring with the box blinking around it, so the graph stays blue and white. SVG paths rather than font glyphs: they scale with the node, stay crisp at any zoom, and cost four short paths per box.

nodes.label: The trail sees skills and instructions
nodes.description: Record which skill and which instructions an agent is acting on, still at no token cost: a UserPromptSubmit hook notes a slash command's name (/plan, /optimize, a user's own — never the prompt's text), PreToolUse notes Claude Code's Skill tool, commands that run the vendored CLIs (plan.mjs, canvas.mjs, analyze.mjs) count toward their skill, and reads of AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or a skill file become 'instruction' lines. The in-app agent's slash commands land the same way.

nodes.label: Every skill each agent has
nodes.description: One scan of the skills the agents in this project can run: Sleipnir's built-ins (registry.mjs) and the user's own in Claude Code (.claude/commands, .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md), Codex (.codex/prompts) and Gemini (.gemini/commands). For each: name, description, file, which agents have it, the CLIs and tools it drives, the folders it writes, and its size in tokens. Frontmatter plus a search for known commands — cheap, cached, read like the other planning data.

nodes.label: SKILLS next to Architecture
nodes.description: A SKILLS mode in the tab's toggle (ARCHITECTURE | SKILLS | HEALTH | PLAN ONLY), drawn by the same graph: the agents, the instruction files they load, their skills, the CLIs and tools each skill drives, and what those touch (.planning, boards, the analyzer, code). The trail runs here too — the corner box lands on the skill in use and the instruction being read, links thicken with the paths agents actually take, and skills nobody uses fade. Watching it shows how an agent gets from your request to the code.

nodes.label: Edit and add skills from the graph
nodes.description: Select a skill and its card shows what it does, which agents have it, its token cost and its text, editable in place; saving writes the skill's own file. New skill: name, description, instructions and which agents get it — Sleipnir writes each agent's format through the same emitters as the built-ins. Changing a built-in writes a project override (.sleipnir/skills/<id>.md) that the scaffolder merges, so updates never overwrite it. Replaces steps 5 and 6 of 'Planning as agent diagnostics'.

nodes.label: Where the agent's effort went
nodes.description: A report computed from the trail, at no token cost: per step and per session — reads per edit, files read again and again, searches whose results went unused, files read but never touched, edit-test-edit loops, time per step, and attention outside the step's files. Drawn as effort heat on the architecture (where the agent's time went) with a short list beside it, and readable by agents through `analyze.mjs trail`, so /optimize can tune its own process as well as the code.

nodes.label: Steer the agent at the moments that matter
nodes.description: Make helping cheap: mark a node 'focus' or 'avoid' for the step in progress, straight from the graph — written onto the step and handed to the agent in list-steps and plan.md, like comments. Sleipnir raises the moments worth a look, from the trail: work outside the step's files, the same file edited over and over while tests keep failing, a long stretch of reading with no edit. The flag shows on the step and in the caption; your comment back is the next thing the agent reads.

nodes.label: Experiment: does the map help agents debug?
nodes.description: A repeatable benchmark on the optimize lab's planted problems (context-menu-lag, react-shop, py-orders, go-inventory, rust-engine) plus seeded bugs with failing tests. Headless Claude Code at the same effort, three runs per condition: plain; Sleipnir's slim instructions with the analyzer map; and /optimize. Measured: whether the cause was found and fixed, turns, tokens, cost, and — from the trail — wrong files read before the right one. Results append to a history file, so every change to instructions, skills or the map shows whether agents got faster or slower over time.

nodes.label: Statuses from the trail
nodes.description: Set step statuses from what agents already do, so they don't spend turns reporting: in progress at the first edit to a step's planned or listed files, testing when a test command runs, done when tests pass after the step's last edit (a commit settles it, as now). Agents report only what can't be inferred — which step, when a file belongs to two, and a one-line note; their report or your toggle always wins over an inference.

nodes.label: One ink, no opacity
nodes.description: Every graph mark in one color — white on dark, black on light — at full strength: nodes, lines, labels, rings, boxes. Status is shape alone (dashed ring proposed, ring in progress, ring in a box testing, dot done, small dot committed); selection is a ring and a heavier line, not a color or a fade. Heat glows and dimming go.

nodes.label: The box holds where the agent is
nodes.description: One steady corner box on the node the agent is on now — no blinking, no fading trail of boxes.

nodes.label: The plan in the left panel
nodes.description: A plan tab lists its steps 1 to n with their status, the plan description above them, and each step opening in place to its description, files, status and activity — so the right panel is only needed for a file or a skill.

nodes.label: Steps open and close
nodes.description: An open step closes again when clicked; only a newly started or newly picked step opens by itself.

nodes.label: Steps on a timeline
nodes.description: Each step's status mark sits on one vertical line, solid through finished work and dashed ahead, with its history as ticks on the same line.

nodes.label: Reading, not commenting
nodes.description: The step list is for reading: status, history and links into the workspace. The comment box goes; agents and the CLI can still comment.

nodes.label: Pinned views
nodes.description: Architecture, Skills and Health open as their own tabs, without a plan: the project, the agents' instructions and skills, and the import health.

nodes.label: The picker as a history
nodes.description: The dropdown lists the pinned views first, then every plan newest first with its date and progress.

nodes.label: A plan opens on its own
nodes.description: The four-way toggle goes; a plan tab shows the plan alone, with an IN PROJECT switch to see it over the architecture.

nodes.label: Planning becomes Agent
nodes.description: The rail and picker name the area for what it shows: the agent's markdown, plans and skills.

nodes.label: Spacing slider
nodes.description: A slider in the graph's bottom right spreads nodes apart — longer links, stronger repulsion — for crowded projects, remembered per viewer.

nodes.label: Details in the left panel
nodes.description: A picked node's card and the effort insights open at the top of the left panel, with a close button; the left panel widens and the right panel goes.

nodes.label: Health on the left
nodes.description: The Health view's report — totals, the selected file, the loops and hot spots — fills the left panel.

nodes.label: Skills listed on the left
nodes.description: The Skills view lists the instruction files with their size, then every skill as a row that opens in place to its card.

nodes.label: A picker that says what it holds
nodes.description: Closed it reads ARCHITECTURE · SKILLS · CHATS; open, VIEWS then CHATS & PLANS, newest first.

nodes.label: Health is an overlay
nodes.description: Health leaves the pinned views and sits beside Effort as one of two overlays, laid over the architecture or a plan in the project; its report opens in the left panel.

nodes.label: Keep CodeMirror off the first load
nodes.description: Planning is on screen at launch, and App → PlanningView → ActivityPanel → DiffView → diffHighlight → codeEditorTheme pulls @codemirror/view (and language) into the first chunk; AgentChat's ToolActivityRow does the same. Load DiffView's highlighter on demand (dynamic import of diffHighlight inside DiffView, plain text until it resolves) so diffs only fetch CodeMirror when one is opened. Moves: heavy packages loaded eagerly 1 → 0; first-load JS should drop by CodeMirror's size (measure with vite build before/after).

nodes.label: Split the backend along its seams
nodes.description: tools/sleipnir-backend.mjs is the top hotspot (score 212, 2435 lines, 77 exports, in 13, out 10, 11 changes) and a god file. It already has three marked sections: agent scaffolding, architecture-aware plan steps, agents reporting progress. Move each into its own module and keep sleipnir-backend.mjs as the thin re-export its 13 importers (vite.config.ts, sleipnir-plan.mjs, tests) already use, so no caller changes. Moves: backend 2435 → ~900 lines, god files 3 → 2, hotspot score down as churn spreads.

nodes.label: Pull boards, pen and pointer out of the canvas ViewModel
nodes.description: src/01_canvas/CanvasView.ViewModel.tsx is 3909 lines with out 30. Its own section markers give the seams: board list/load/autosave/staged files/external change (≈ lines 583-997), pen + point editing (≈1020-1305), pointer interaction (≈1306-2142). Extract each into a hook in src/01_canvas/hooks/ beside usePanZoom; the ViewModel composes them. Also cuts re-render scope: pen and pointer state stop living beside board persistence. Moves: ViewModel 3909 → <1500 lines, out 30 → ~15.

nodes.label: Move activityLog next to its users
nodes.description: src/00_planning/graph/activityLog.ts is imported only by src/00_planning/* panels (100% of its connections) and imports only graph/types. Move it (and its test) to src/00_planning/activityLog.ts and update the 6 importers. Moves: possibly misplaced 6 → 5.

nodes.label: Move schemaAdapters into chatProviders
nodes.description: electron/agent/schemaAdapters.cjs is used by the four electron/chatProviders/* files (80% of its connections) plus chat.cjs. Move it and its test into electron/chatProviders/. Moves: possibly misplaced 5 → 4.

nodes.label: Delete the two dead source files
nodes.description: Nothing imports src/01_canvas/panels/CanvasComponentsPanel.tsx or src/app/DesignSystem/treeSelection.ts (checked with grep across src, electron and tools). Delete both. The other two unreferenced files are optimizeLab fixtures and stay. Moves: unreferenced 4 → 2.

nodes.label: Same camera controls in 3D as in 2D
nodes.description: 2D already does this (usePanZoom): wheel pans up/down, Shift+wheel or a trackpad pans sideways, Ctrl/Cmd+wheel zooms at the cursor, Space+left-drag and middle-drag pan, right-drag does nothing. Bring the 3D viewport in line: replace OrbitControls' defaults (left orbits, right pans, wheel dollies) with left = select only, right-drag = orbit (perspective view only, as now), Space+left-drag and middle-drag = pan, wheel = pan along the screen, Ctrl/Cmd+wheel = zoom toward the cursor. The pan/zoom math lives in a pure module so it's tested without a GPU.

nodes.label: One position for 2D and 3D
nodes.description: Today a top-level layer's 2D position (rect.x/y) and its 3D placement (space.position) are separate once it's placed, so moving it in 3D doesn't move it in 2D and vice versa. Make the placement the source for placed layers: a 3D move updates rect.x/y to the front-view projection of the plane's origin, and a 2D move (drag, nudge, align, X/Y fields) writes space.position x/y, keeping z. Unplaced layers are unchanged (they already sit at defaultPlacement(rect)).

nodes.label: The front-view projection
nodes.description: The 2D board is the 3D Front orthographic camera: board px = (X, -Y) × PX_PER_METER, depth dropped. For a flat layer that's an affine map from its plane to the board, the first two columns of its rotation × scale plus the projected origin, so it fits the existing Mat type and CSS matrix(). Add frontMatrix(placement) and use it in boardMatrixOf for placed top-level layers, so every ring, handle, hit test and guide already built on boardMatrixOf follows. Edge-on planes (|det| ≈ 0) are flagged so they can be drawn and picked as a line.

nodes.label: Flat layers drawn as the front view sees them
nodes.description: A placed layer renders in 2D through its front matrix (CSS matrix(), board-only; emitted code is untouched), so a plane turned about Y squashes horizontally and one turned about X and Y becomes a rhombus. Children inherit through the DOM. The selection ring and handles draw the projected parallelogram rather than a rotated box (orientedFrom assumes no skew), resize/rotate handles map drags back through the inverse matrix, and edge-on layers show as a hairline that can still be clicked.

nodes.label: Solids drawn as their projected faces
nodes.description: An extruded, revolved or swept layer can't be drawn by an affine map, so 2D draws its mesh through the same front camera: triangles projected to the board, back faces culled, sorted far to near, each shaded from the 3D view's key light, so a rotated cube reads as a shaded diamond/hexagon exactly as the 3D Front view shows it. The mesh builders (layerMesh, sweptMesh, sweepsAlong, surfaceOf) move out of the lazy 3D chunk into scene3d so the board can use them without three.js. Hit-testing and the selection ring use the projected outline's bounds.

nodes.label: Edit a placed layer straight-on
nodes.description: With 2D as the front view, a sketch on the Top or Side plane is edge-on and can't be drawn on. Double-click (or Enter) on a placed layer enters plane-edit: the board shows just that layer's plane straight-on, other placed layers ghosted with the cross-plane guides (scene3d/sketchPlane.ts) so the views still line up, and Esc returns to the front view. This keeps today's Top/Side sketching workflow.

nodes.label: Retire 'the 2D board is always straight-on'
nodes.description: The model, inspector and 3D view all say the 2D board ignores placement. Update those statements and hints to the new rule (2D is the Front view; plane-edit shows a plane straight-on): CanvasNode.space's doc comment, PlaneSection's hint and Reset tooltip, Viewport3D's header comment, and the plane guides that now only draw in plane-edit.

nodes.label: Verify in the running app
nodes.description: Over CDP in the dev app: an extruded square rotated 45° about Y then 35° about X shows in 2D as the same shaded hexagon the 3D Front view renders (screenshot both at matching zoom); moving it with the gizmo moves it in 2D and dragging it in 2D moves it in 3D; scroll, Ctrl+scroll, Space+drag behave the same in both; right-drag orbits only in 3D Persp.

nodes.label: Pick a solid's faces, edges and points
nodes.description: Requested 2026-11-02: in 3D and in 2D, hover and click picks one face of a solid, e.g. a cube's top face turned toward the viewer, and shows it as its own editable shape: its edges and vertices drawn (projected in 2D), points selectable and draggable. Faces map back to what built them: an extrude's caps are the layer's outline (dragging a cap vertex moves that outline point, in the plane via the inverse front matrix), a side face is one outline segment swept by the depth (its edges move the two points, its far edge moves depth), a revolve's faces trace back to profile points. Needs frontFaces / the mesh builders to tag each triangle with its source face (cap/side + outline index), a face-pick in 2D alongside solidAt, and the same in the 3D viewport via raycast faceIndex. Should line up with the 3D creation plan's 'Point selection' and 'Edit mode: vertices, edges, faces' steps rather than duplicate them.

nodes.label: Sketches and Objects in the board
nodes.description: The model change everything else builds on. A Sketch is a top-level frame (all of Figma: frames, auto layout, components, text, vectors) with sketch: { plane: PlaneRef }, where it sits in 3D. An Object is a part: { id, name, features: Feature[], placement }, and a Feature is extrude | revolve | sweep | loft | boolean, each naming the sketch (and which of its closed shapes, its 'regions') it consumes, plus depth/axis/op (new body, add, subtract, intersect). Today's per-layer space + solid fields migrate on load: a layer with a solid becomes a sketch plus an object with one feature; a placed layer without one becomes a sketch on a custom plane. Old boards keep opening; CANVAS_SCHEMA_VERSION bumps.

nodes.label: Bodies with named faces, edges and points
nodes.description: Evaluate an Object's feature list into a body whose every face, edge and vertex has a stable name saying where it came from, the way Onshape keeps 'Extrude 1 > end cap' alive across edits: { feature, role: start-cap | end-cap | side, sketch node id, outline segment or point index }. Triangles keep the face they belong to, so a click (a 3D raycast's faceIndex, or a 2D projected triangle) resolves to a face, its edges and its corners. Built on geometry/modifiers' extrude, revolve and sweep, plus booleans between bodies. This is what makes 'pick the top face' and 'drag that corner' answerable at all.

nodes.label: Planes a sketch can sit on
nodes.description: PlaneRef resolution: the three default planes (Front, Top, Right, named as Onshape names them), an offset or angled plane from one of them, or a face of an object (by its stable name from the previous step). A sketch on a face moves when the face moves: extrude a box, sketch a circle on its top, extrude that, then change the box's depth and the second feature rides along. Replaces free-floating space for sketches; the front view and plane edit (scene3d/frontView.ts, planeEdit.ts) read the resolved placement.

nodes.label: +Sketch and +Object in the left panel
nodes.description: Under the board picker (it stays the panel's one search and board switcher, per the left-rail rule), two create buttons become the main way to add things. + Sketch asks where: Front, Top, Right, or 'pick a face' (in 3D), then opens it in sketch mode. + Object offers icons: from a sketch (Extrude, Revolve, Sweep, Loft, using the selected sketch or asking for one) or a starter shape (Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Plane), each made as a sketch plus a feature so it edits the same way. 'New board' stays in the picker's create row.

nodes.label: Layers: Sketches, and Objects with their feature list
nodes.description: The layers panel splits in two, like Onshape's feature list over its parts list, in Figma's look. Sketches: each sketch frame with its layer tree, as today. Objects: each part, expanding to its features in order (Sketch 1 > Extrude 1 > Sketch 2 > Revolve 1); clicking a feature selects it, double-clicking a sketch opens sketch mode, dragging reorders (rebuilding after), an eye hides. A sketch a feature consumes shows under that feature, as in Onshape.

nodes.label: Sketch mode: Figma on the sketch's plane
nodes.description: Plane edit (scene3d/planeEdit.ts) becomes sketch mode in Onshape's sense: open a sketch (double-click it, its tree row, or + Sketch) and the board shows that plane face on with every Figma tool, the bodies it sits on ghosted and projected onto the plane so you can draw against their edges, plus the cross-plane guides. Finish sketch (or Esc) closes it and the features using it rebuild. Plane edit's chip becomes the Onshape-style sketch bar: the sketch's name, its plane, Finish.

nodes.label: Sketch mode in 3D: the board laid over the scene
nodes.description: The seamless half: opening a sketch in the 3D view turns the camera to face its plane and locks it orthographic, and the live 2D board (DOM, transparent background) is drawn on top, its pan and zoom driving the 3D camera, so you draw with Figma's tools while the solids show behind. Finishing swings the camera back. This is the 'add 2D sketches into a 3D environment' moment, without two editors.

nodes.label: What editing a face, edge or point changes
nodes.description: The rules, as pure functions, from a named element and a move to a change in the sketch or feature that made it: a cap's corner moves that sketch point (on the plane, through the inverse plane matrix); dragging a side face pushes or pulls its outline segment; an end cap pulled along its normal changes the extrude's depth (push/pull, as in Onshape or SketchUp); a revolve's faces move profile points; an edge moves its two points. Anything with no source (a boolean seam) says so rather than guessing. The 3D creation plan's 'Editable meshes' step is the escape hatch for free-form mesh editing beyond this.

nodes.label: Selection modes and hotkeys
nodes.description: Blender's select modes on any object, in 3D and in the 2D front view: Tab toggles object and edit mode, 1 / 2 / 3 pick points, edges or faces, click selects, Shift adds, A all, Alt+A none, box-drag selects in edit mode. Hover highlights the face or edge under the cursor; selected points draw as dots, edges as lines, faces tinted. Figma's keys stay while a sketch is open (V, F, R, O, P, T); Blender's apply in 3D and on objects; a ? overlay lists both. Picking uses the named triangles from 'Bodies with named faces, edges and points'.

nodes.label: Grab, rotate, scale and push/pull
nodes.description: Blender's modal transforms on whatever is selected: G grab, R rotate, S scale, then X / Y / Z to lock an axis (twice for local), type a number for an exact amount, Enter or click to confirm, Esc or right-click to cancel. On an object they move its placement; on faces, edges and points they go through 'What editing a face, edge or point changes', so dragging a cube's top face up deepens the extrude and its corners stay on the sketch. The gizmo (viewport/TransformGizmo.tsx) does the same by mouse.

nodes.label: 3D tools and the feature inspector
nodes.description: 3D's toolbar is Onshape's feature set in Figma's style and words: Select, Sketch, Extrude, Revolve, Sweep, Loft, Combine (union / subtract / intersect), Plane, Move. Choosing one with a sketch or face selected starts that feature with a live preview; the inspector shows its fields (depth, direction, both sides, add or subtract into which object, axis, angle) as Onshape's feature dialog does, with OK and Cancel. SolidSection's per-layer solid controls fold into it.

nodes.label: The front view draws objects from their bodies
nodes.description: The 2D board stops drawing solids per layer (scene3d/sceneMeshes.ts projectedSolidsOf) and draws every Object's evaluated body through the front camera with its named faces, so picking, hover and edit-mode dots work in 2D too. Sketches draw as frames on their planes as now (squashed, sheared or edge-on); a sketch a feature has consumed draws as a thin outline. Retires drawsAsSolid.

nodes.label: Agents and files speak sketches and objects
nodes.description: The canvas CLI agents use (/frame and /component through tools/agentSkills/vendor/canvas.mjs, copied into projects as .sleipnir/canvas.mjs) and the board file learn sketches, planes, objects and features, so an AI can say 'sketch a circle on the top face of Box and extrude it 2 cm' and Sleipnir builds it. The /frame and /component skill text explains the two kinds. Emitted 2D component code is unchanged: a sketch is still a frame.

nodes.label: Verify in the running app
nodes.description: Over CDP in the dev app with a scratch project: + Object > Box; pick its top face (Tab, 3, click) in 3D and in 2D; G, Z, 20 raises it and the depth changes; + Sketch on that face, draw a circle with Figma's ellipse tool in sketch mode (2D and 3D), Finish, Extrude it; change the box's depth and the circle's extrude follows; select a corner (1) and drag it, and the sketch point moves; an old board with per-layer solids opens migrated.

nodes.label: What goes where: left panel, toolbox, right panel
nodes.description: One rule for the canvas, 2D and 3D alike, written down so every later step follows it. Left panel: what's in the scene, sketches and objects with their layers and features, and adding a new sketch to the list (+ Sketch); it never shapes anything. Toolbox: every tool that draws or shapes, grouped by what it acts on: select and edit-mode picks (points, edges, faces), 2D drawing (frame, shapes, pen, text), 3D shaping (extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, combine, plane), starter shapes (box, cylinder, sphere, cone, torus, polygon), transform (move, rotate, scale), and later sculpt brushes. Right panel: the settings of whatever is selected, a layer's fill and layout, a feature's depth and axis, a point's position; it never creates. Each tool lives in exactly one place. The doc also maps Figma's and Onshape's names for each.

nodes.label: The toolbox in 3D: shaping tools and starter shapes
nodes.description: Brought forward so each step can be seen in the app. The board's toolbox gets its 3D groups beside the 2D ones (one toolbox, the groups shown for the view you're in): Extrude, Revolve, Sweep and Loft act on the selected sketch (or ask for one) and create or extend an Object; starter shapes, Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Cone, Torus and Polygon (n sides), each made as a sketch plus a feature (a sphere is a revolved half circle, a polygon an extruded n-gon) so they edit like anything else. Tools are defined once in a registry both views read, with their key, icon and which view they belong to. Settings for what a tool made appear in the right panel (the inspector's Solid section until the feature inspector lands).

nodes.label: Show the whole architecture in the graph
nodes.description: Fixes missing nodes when Sleipnir opens itself: scopeArchitecture keeps at most 300 files (max=300) and folds the rest into depth-2 folder nodes; Sleipnir has ~470 code files plus docs/assets, so most of the graph collapses. Count only source files toward the cap, raise it (~1500), and with no plan focus show everything instead of folders. Moves: files drawn on Sleipnir ~300 -> all ~470.

Await only the first-shown view, warm the rest on idle, and keep three.js behind the lazy Viewport3D chunk. Add a test that fails if an eager module imports three/@react-three. Moves: chunks awaited at boot 6 -> 1.
